name: The Quiet
summary: You cannot die here. Something else can happen to you instead, and it is worse, and it is what most of the creatures in the world already are.
body: You cannot die in Nangijala. That door is behind you and it does not open twice. New stars find this reassuring for about a season.

It does not mean nothing can happen to you. You can be broken — knocked about past the point of holding a shape — and it is as unpleasant as it sounds and it is not an ending. What is left of you goes where the remembering is thickest, which in practice means the nearest fire somebody is tending, and puts itself back together beside it over a few hours. You keep what you were carrying. You lose a little of what you were thinking about. Nobody here treats a fight as final, and everybody here knows exactly how far it is to the nearest lit fire.

What can still happen to you is this. You can be forgotten — by everyone else, and then, in the end, by yourself — until there is nothing holding your shape but habit. It takes a long time and it does not hurt at any point, which is the part people find hard to hear.
It goes in four stages, and they have been called the same four things for as long as anybody has been counting.

You begin Bright. You know who you were and you can say it: your name, your work, the face of somebody you loved, the road home. Most people who fall are Bright for a very long time, particularly if somebody is telling them.

Then you Fade. The particulars go first, and they go so gently you cannot catch them at it. You know that you loved someone. You cannot produce the face. You know there was a road home and you could not now say which direction it ran. A faded person is entirely themselves, and entirely present, and simply has less and less to say about it.

Then there is Habit, and this is where it stops being sad and starts being frightening, because at some point the person is gone and the behaviour is still running. A thing that still walks its round. A thing that still guards its bridge, faithfully, for a keeper whose name went out of the world before it did. A thing that still comes home in the evening to a house that is not there any more and stands in the place where the door used to be.
This is what almost everything you will meet in the wild already is.

It is worth saying plainly, because new stars arrive with ideas about monsters. The creatures out there are not wicked. Very nearly none of them chose anything. Some are shapes that outlasted their occupants and kept doing the last thing they were doing. Others never had an occupant at all, and this world will be explaining those to you for some time. Either way they will come at you for reasons that stopped being reasons a long while back. Do not hate them. They are what happens.

And then, at the end, the Quiet. The shape lets go. There is no body and no grave, because there was no death; the thing simply stops being anywhere, and afterwards the place it was seems slightly wider than it should. People who have watched it happen say the worst part is how ordinary it looks.

The Quiet is what this world is afraid of. Not the creatures, not the cave, not the winter. Every fire, every rota, every argument between the tellers and the Chroniclers, every stranger who walks half a night to meet a falling star — all of it is the same species of answer to the same single question.
Which is: who is going to remember me, and for how long, and will they do it out loud.
